headlines.title: AI shopping agents are having a moment, but Amazon and a growing number of sites threaten to stunt their growth
headlines.summary: AI shopping agents from OpenAI, Meta, Google and Instinct promise to help users shop, but they're hitting roadblocks at Amazon and other retailers.
headlines.article_text: AI shopping agents from OpenAI, Meta, Google hit retailer blocks Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AI shopping agents are growing in popularity, but the rollout is messy and consumers might not see all their retail options. AI companies, retailers, financial institutions and other industries have announced an alphabet soup of rules to make it easier for agents to transact on websites. Instinct CEO Noah Shinn acknowledged the challenges. "We can obviously move very fast and certain businesses cannot," he told CNBC. "So, how can we collaborate with them?" Maia Bittner urgently needed to replace her car's windshield wipers. So last month, she turned to Meta 's Muse personal artificial intelligence agent. Bittner, chief product officer at fintech startup Imprint, gave Muse the greenlight to buy some wipers on her behalf from AutoZone. Or so she thought. About 17 hours later, she got a notification from her Muse agent, saying AutoZone canceled her order due to an unspecified error. "Honestly, the most reliable path now is you ordering on Amazon yourself," Muse said, according to a screenshot of the message. The interaction encapsulates the current messy and complicated landscape of agentic shopping apps, the AI tools that can make purchases on behalf of users. Over the past year, tech companies such as OpenAI , Meta, Google and Instinct have introduced versions of personal agents that promise to take the hassle out of browsing and buying online. The rollout has been far from smooth. While some major retailers, such as Walmart and Sephora, have opened up their sites to agents, companies including Amazon, eBay , United Airlines and Kohl's limit what actions agents can take or block them outright. Others have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong. "It's a very mixed bag," Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester, said in an interview. "It means that a consumer who's using an agent to shop and browse and learn is not going to see the full set of options because some websites are unavailable." The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear. Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April. Retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals . Earlier this month, Shopify President Harley Finkelstein predicted this year would be the "first holiday season" where AI-driven shopping goes mainstream. "I think last year we saw AI influence more in discovery," Finkelstein told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "I think now we're going to see more of that conversion." Patchwork of permissions For users hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable. Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers such as Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August by agent security company Billions Network . Amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The company rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders. In September, the company also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity , accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the company expects "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers. Bots encounter issues even when retailers welcome them in. They often fumble through webpages and get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a Captcha test and continue browsing. A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks, such as buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study. Bittner said she is a "big believer" in AI agents' potential. Earlier this year, she said, she was delighted when Perplexity's shopping agent found and purchased a pair of Adidas sneakers that were sold out for months. Other experiences have been clumsier. Last week, she said, she asked Meta's Muse to help her find a Jellycat octopus plushie for her kids. It suggested a product marked 75% off from "Crazy Hobby Supply," a retailer she'd never heard of and that didn't appear to have any reviews, she said. "I sort of trust Google to only surface sites that are not scams to me in their sponsored ads," Bittner said. "In the same way, I want AI to only surface to me websites that are not scams. I don't think we're there yet." Users have reported mishaps with other AI tools , including one case where Instinct's text-based agent booked a hotel and signed up for a loyalty program without the consumer's consent. Many retailers are approaching agents cautiously because they're concerned about fraudulent bot activity. San Francisco-based Skyfire is trying to solve that problem by arming retailers with more data to identify which bots are visiting their site and to verify that a human has actually consented to let an agent buy a product on their behalf. A commuter walks past Meta Muse ads displayed on screens at a subway station in New York, Oct. 29, 2026. Jeenah Moon | Reuters Typically, when a human visits a website, there are "all kinds of signals" to prove it's not a fraudulent user, Skyfire CEO Amir Sarhangi said in an interview. None of those things are available to retailers when an agent accesses their site, Sarhangi said. Agents might appear even more suspicious because they mask their IP address or origin via data centers, and they often use one-time, virtual cards to check out. "So we talked to a lot of merchants and banks and financial institutions, and the things they told us were: We want to know who the end user is, and we want to know it's a real human," Sarhangi said. "We want to know who these agents are, because we're not going to just let willy-nilly anybody do these types of transactions, and we need a way to kind of verify that." AI companies, retailers, financial institutions and other industries have announced an alphabet soup of "protocols," rules that propose ways to make it easier for agents to transact on websites. There's yet to be a broad consensus around who takes responsibility when an agent purchase goes sideways. American Express in April said it would protect eligible customers "from charges related to AI agent error." Stripe, whose Link digital wallet is integrated with Muse, protects some agent purchases and offers a "refund guarantee." Others are more wary. Last month, JPMorgan Chase blocked external agents from operating on behalf of customers, citing security concerns. Best Buy is among several retailers that deem users responsible for agent purchases in their terms of service. Best Buy says it views those transactions "as if you performed them yourself." headlines.article_text: SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push: Bloomberg Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points SAP is weighing at least 10,000 job cuts as it reshapes its software business for the AI era, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "We are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC. The report comes as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data." In this article SAP Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The headquarters of SAP AG, Germany's largest software company, on Jan. 8, 2013, in Walldorf, Germany. Thomas Lohnes | Getty Images News | Getty Images SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday , citing people familiar with the matter. "The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC. "As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation." The company did not provide any further details on potential job cuts. The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data." "SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said. "Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on." Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations. Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model. In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus. The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining. Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported. In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue. watch now VIDEO 6:50 06:50 SAP CEO Christian Klein says there are more A.I. use cases coming down the pipeline Closing Bell: Overtime The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy . This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct. The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.
